question: What kind of infections are treated using antibacterial drugs?
explanation: Spot on! Antibacterials are designed specifically to target bacteria, while leaving viruses and fungi alone. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h1)

question: Why do we always tell patients to finish their full course of antibiotics, even if they feel better?

options.A: It lowers the patient's blood pressure dangerously fast
options.B: It causes the drug to instantly accumulate in the liver
options.C: It immediately destroys all normal flora in the body
options.D: It leaves the strongest bacteria alive to cause stronger infections

explanation: Stopping early is a big no-no! It kills off the weak bacteria and leaves the tough ones behind to multiply and cause drug resistance. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h1)

question: What do we call a drug's special superpower of harming bacteria without damaging human cells?
explanation: You got it! Selective toxicity means the drug safely attacks unique parts of the bacteria while sparing our own human cells. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h2)

question: How do medications like penicillin actually destroy bacterial cells?

options.B: By breaking down the protective cell wall
options.C: By increasing the acidity of the blood
options.D: By blocking the replication of human DNA

explanation: Think of the cell wall as the bacteria's armor. Penicillin weakens this wall so it bursts open and dies! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h2)

question: What is the main job of a bacteriostatic drug?

options.A: Neutralizing bacterial toxins in the blood

explanation: Bacteriostatic drugs press 'pause' on bacterial growth and let the patient's immune system clean up the rest. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h3)

question: If a patient has a very weak immune system, which type of drug do they urgently need to fight an infection?
explanation: Since their immune system can't finish the job, they need bactericidal drugs to directly kill the bacteria for them. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h3)

question: Why are narrow-spectrum antibiotics preferred when you know the exact germ causing the trouble?

options.A: They work much faster than broad-spectrum drugs
options.B: They never cause allergic reactions in patients
options.C: They can be taken without water
options.D: They cause less harm to normal body flora

explanation: Spot on! Narrow-spectrum is like a sniper rifle—it hits only the bad bug and leaves your healthy friendly bacteria alone. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h4)

question: What nasty surprise can happen when a patient stays on broad-spectrum antibiotics for too long?

options.A: Total failure of pancreatic enzyme production
options.C: Permanent loss of the sense of taste

explanation: When you wipe out good flora, opportunistic bugs like fungi or *C. diff* take over and cause a superinfection. Good to keep in mind for clinicals! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h4)

question: What is the sneaky trick that bacterial enzymes like beta-lactamase pull off?

options.A: They help bacteria digest human red blood cells
options.C: They speed up bacterial cell division
options.D: They create a thick capsule around the cell

explanation: Beta-lactamases are defense weapons for bacteria; they chop up the antibiotic before it can do its job. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h5)

question: What is the main goal of antimicrobial stewardship programs in hospitals?

options.A: To ensure all patients receive broad-spectrum coverage daily
options.B: To eliminate the need for bacterial laboratory cultures
options.C: To promote the correct and careful use of antibacterial drugs
options.D: To find cheaper generic substitutes for every medication

explanation: Stewardship is all about making sure antibiotics are used wisely so they don't lose their power over time. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h5)

question: As a nurse, what is the most important check you must do before giving a patient a new antibacterial drug?

options.B: Weighing the patient on a digital scale

explanation: Safety first! Always check for allergies so you don't trigger a severe, life-threatening reaction like anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h6)

question: If a patient is on an antibiotic that can harm the kidneys, which lab results should you closely watch?

options.B: Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen

explanation: You got it! Creatinine and BUN are your best indicators of how well the kidneys are filtering waste. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h6)

question: A doctor orders a wound culture and an IV antibiotic for a new patient. Which order of steps is correct?

options.A: The order of these two actions does not matter clinically
options.B: Collect the wound culture first, then start the antibiotic
options.C: Give half the antibiotic dose, collect the culture, then give the rest
options.D: Administer the antibiotic first, then collect the culture the next day

explanation: Always culture before you treat! If you start the antibiotic first, it might kill the bacteria before the lab can catch it. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h7)

question: Which clinical sign tells you that an antibiotic is successfully beating the infection?

options.A: Elevation in patient blood pressure readings
options.B: Complete disappearance of normal skin flora
options.C: Increase in patient appetite within one hour
options.D: Reduction in fever and white blood cell count

explanation: Brilliant! Watching the fever drop and WBC count return to normal is a classic nursing win. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h7)
